Permitting reform · project timelines

Project timeline savings under BAAJA

The overwhelming majority of time savings in BAAJA come when reviews experience delays and challenges.

The bill has a range of potential time savings across different energy infrastructure projects

Months sooner if agencies meet deadlinesMonths sooner with delays and challenges

Each archetype is meant to be illustrative of how BAAJA could change project timelines and is a composite of recorded cases. They are not representative of projects currently proposed or being built. These savings are not guaranteed across all projects. They count only months, not projects that current law stopped and the bill might have let proceed.

Pick a project type and a scenario. In the timeline, the grey bar is current law and the colored bar below it is BAAJA, and the chip by a step shows how much sooner it ends under BAAJA. A black tick marks the median of recorded cases for a step, where one exists. Hover or tap any bar for its basis and source.

Project type
Scenario

Each bar is one provision's share of the months this project saves in the chosen scenario; the bars run end to end and add up to the total. Provisions overlap, so each share is the provision's average contribution across every order in which they could take effect. Hover or tap a bar for what it saves alone and added last.

What's included

Project-specific EISs for the six project types in CEQ's 2010 to 2024 data, plus one solar EIS missing from it (Crimson), three EISs still under review and 25 BLM geothermal exploration reviews.

How the replay works

Each project's recorded dates are replayed under the bill's limits: the EIS capped at 28 months from the NOI (the 2-year deadline plus a 4-month sponsor suit), the decision at 2 months after the final EIS, BLM's wait before the NOI at the bill's deadlines, and test-well permits at 2 months. Months the bill would excuse or not cut, such as a developer's redesign or a funding lapse that began before a deadline, stay in.

How to read it

Each row is one project, sorted by months saved. The grey bar is the recorded review, from the NOI (or, where the replay counts a wait before the NOI, the start of that wait) to the federal decision; the blue bar below ends where the decision would have come under BAAJA, and the chip by the name gives the difference. The replays stop at the federal decision, so they leave out state siting and the FERC backstop permit (Sec. 2101), where most of the transmission archetype's gain comes from; to the federal decision, that archetype gains 64 months. Hover or tap a bar for its dates and why it ran long.

Project type

The replays stop at the federal decision, because the records do not show when projects were built. They assume agencies and developers behave as they did, except that developers refuse extensions they did not cause; on the Permitting Dashboard developers usually agreed to them. Reviews still under way use the agency's current schedule. Every project, with its sources, is in the CSV.

Limitations

  • Composite projects. Each archetype combines steps from several real cases. No single project followed every step as drawn.
  • Review scope. The charts review the whole line or pipeline under both laws, so they leave out any gain from limiting historic review to the federally controlled segment (Sec. 2301). The sensitivity table in the data download sizes it for the transmission line.
  • Geothermal wells. The charts keep development wells in the plant's EA under both laws, so they leave out any gain from Sec. 2229's exemption for wells at recently drilled pads. The sensitivity table in the data download sizes it at 0 to 10 months in service.
  • No change in behavior. The replays and charts apply the bill's deadlines to past dates. They do not account for agencies delaying completeness notices to avoid the clock, sponsors agreeing to extensions, or reviews written to a deadline drawing more suits or remands.
  • Survivors only. The replays include projects that reached an EIS, or for geothermal exploration a BLM review, and, nearly all, a decision. Projects that stalled before an NOI, where the bill's NOI deadlines might matter most, are absent.
  • Decision, not service. The replays measure months to the federal decision. The archetype charts carry on to the in-service date. The replays therefore leave out state siting and the FERC backstop permit (Sec. 2101), which give the transmission archetype most of its 96 months; to the federal decision it gains 64, against 60.7 for the largest replay (Bordertown to California, a 10-mile, 120 kV line).
  • The EIS clock in the replays. The replays start the 2-year clock at the NOI, because the records rarely date a completeness notice. Under the bill it starts at the earlier completeness notice, so the replays' EIS cap is generous to current law and understates the saving.
  • Causes from public records. Agencies rarely record why a step ran long; on the Permitting Dashboard, reasons are recorded for fewer than 1 in 5 delayed milestones. For many checked projects the record names who held the review but not why.
  • Date conventions. CEQ's final EIS date is EPA's notice of availability. CEQ's decision dates were checked against decision records and corrected where they differ. Dates recorded only by month or year are counted from the period's end. Most geothermal exploration start dates are proxies: the operator's plan or notice, or BLM's earliest dated record of the proposal.
  • Pending projects. Bonanza, Mosey and Vineyard Mid-Atlantic use the agency's current schedule, which may change.
  • Collection method. Records were collected with the use of AI and authors, checking second sources when available.
  • Bill text. The analysis reflects the September 30, 2026 text. Amendments would change the bill_provisions table in the data download and possibly the charts.
